title: Jalapeño: OpenAI and Broadcom's Inference Chip
hook: OpenAI co-designed a custom chip — Jalapeño — built only for running LLMs, betting that inference-specific silicon beats general GPUs on cost and scale.
key_points: Jalapeño is purpose-built for inference — serving trained models — not for training them.
It was co-designed with Broadcom, signaling frontier labs moving toward custom silicon.
The stated goals are better performance, energy efficiency, and scale for deploying large models.
Specializing the chip to the inference workload is what lets it target lower cost per token than a general-purpose GPU.
content_html: OpenAI and Broadcom unveiled Jalapeño, a custom AI chip built specifically for LLM inference. Unlike a general-purpose GPU that handles both training and serving, Jalapeño targets only the inference workload — running already-trained models — with the goal of improving performance, energy efficiency, and scale.
extra_html:
What it is

Jalapeño is an inference accelerator co-designed by OpenAI and Broadcom. Inference is the act of serving a model to users — every chat reply or completion. By narrowing the chip's job to that one workload, the design can be tuned for it more aggressively than a chip that must also support the flexibility training requires.

Why it matters

For a lab serving models to hundreds of millions of users, the cumulative cost of inference can dominate the budget far more than one-time training runs. A frontier lab co-designing its own inference silicon is a bet on controlling that cost, efficiency, and supply rather than depending entirely on general-purpose GPUs. See OpenAI's announcement for details.

related.title: NVIDIA Blackwell (B200 / GB200)
related.hook: Blackwell is the chip the 2025 frontier ran on: a two-die GPU with an FP4 transformer engine, built to train and serve trillion-parameter models.

related.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU
related.hook: Google built a custom chip whose heart is a 256x256 grid of 8-bit multiply-accumulate units - and in production it ran neural-net inference roughly 15-30x faster than the GPUs and CPUs of its day.

related.title: The Hardware Lottery
related.hook: A research idea can win not because it is genuinely better, but because it happens to fit the hardware and software we already have. Sara Hooker calls this the hardware lottery.

flashcards.prompt: How does an inference-optimized chip like Jalapeño differ in purpose from a training GPU?
flashcards.back_html: It specializes in serving trained models — running forward passes cheaply and at scale — rather than the heavier, more flexible workload of training them.

flashcards.prompt: What does a frontier lab co-designing its own inference chip signal?

choices.text: A push to control inference cost, efficiency, and hardware supply instead of relying solely on general-purpose GPUs
That training models no longer requires any GPUs
That model architectures have stopped changing

flashcards.explanation_html: Custom silicon tuned for one workload trades flexibility for efficiency — a bet that pays off when you run that workload at enormous scale, as labs serving models do.
